pointers.sentence: A view is defined by how it is used, and the use is a single line of `BaseHandler._get_response`, or of its asynchronous twin under ASGI: the callable that the resolver returned is called with the request, then the positional arguments, then the keyword arguments (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response`).
`path` and `re_path` take whatever is callable and keep it as `URLPattern.callback` (`django/urls/conf.py:_path`).
The resolver hands each back as it was given, an Almanac and a `functools.partial` (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLPattern.resolve`).

For a subclass of `View` the system check `"urls.E009"` reports the mistake ([The URL checks, and listing the patterns](../urls/checks.md#the-four-checks-tagged-urls)), and a request routed to it all the same ends as a 500: the handler calls the class with the request, and `View.__init__`, which takes keyword arguments only, raises a `TypeError` (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLPattern._check_callback`, `django/views/generic/base.py:View.__init__`).

Each raises a `ValueError` whose message names the view (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.check_response`).

The check does not follow `"view_class"`, which would have named the class; [`View.as_view` and dispatch](as-view.md) tells why the function's name is left alone (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.as_view`).

With `CommonMiddleware` installed, that middleware's `process_response` is the first to touch the object, the failure happens inside the chain, and the client gets an ordinary 500 (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.get_response`).

An `Exception` raised by a view is offered to the `process_exception` hooks, and if none of them answers, `convert_exception_to_response` turns it into a response according to the exception's class, a 404 for `Http404` from Django's own error view ([How an exception becomes a response](../handlers/exceptions.md)) (`django/core/handlers/exception.py:response_for_exception`).

So the view carries an attribute, a **mark**, set by a decorator, by `as_view`, or by the admin site for its own views, which the code that needs to know looks for with `getattr` and a default, or with `hasattr` (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view`, `django/urls/resolvers.py:ResolverMatch.__init__`).

| `"_non_atomic_requests"`, a set | `non_atomic_requests` in `django/db/transaction.py` | `BaseHandler.make_view_atomic` | the database aliases for which the view is not wrapped in a transaction, though `"ATOMIC_REQUESTS"` is on |

It does when each decorator outside copies the wrapped function's attributes onto its own wrapper, which `functools.wraps` does, and every wrapper made in `django/views/decorators/` is passed through it.
Then an object with no `__name__` is named by its class and its class's module, and anything else by its own name and module (`django/urls/resolvers.py:ResolverMatch.__init__`).
That path is what a debug page prints as the view an exception was raised in (`django/views/debug.py:get_caller`).

`URLPattern.lookup_str` is a second dotted path, worked out by other rules: it looks through a `functools.partial` to the function inside and through `"view_class"` to the class, and the resolver collects it from every pattern, which the admin's documentation consults to tell whether a dotted name is that of a view of the URLconf ([Reversing a name](../urls/reversing.md#the-tables)) (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLPattern.lookup_str`).
